scenes.title: hook (a lower resting rate doesn't win races)

voiceover.text: So, what does training change inside the body? You met the start of the answer in Year 11. A trained cyclist rests at forty-eight beats a minute and an untrained person at seventy-two, because each trained beat is bigger. But a low resting heart rate doesn't win races. Predict what training changes at maximum effort. Then name one change outside the heart, and say whether the lungs grow.

Here's the recall. Cardiac output, the blood the heart pumps each minute, is heart rate times stroke volume, the blood pumped per beat. Endurance training enlarges the left ventricle's chamber, and its wall strengthens to match. So it fills more, and stroke volume rises. At rest the body needs about the same output either way, so fewer beats are needed. Seventy-two times seventy and forty-eight times a hundred and five both give about five thousand millilitres a minute. Same output, split differently. Now the new part: what does that buy when the body works hard?

scenes.title: exercise, maximum, oxygen and the lungs

voiceover.text: Now exercise. At the same light workload, both need the same cardiac output, but the trained heart meets it with fewer, bigger beats, so its heart rate is lower and it sits further below its ceiling. That's why the same session feels easier. At maximum, the picture changes. Maximum heart rate is set mostly by age, and training doesn't raise it. But stroke volume is much higher, so maximum cardiac output is much higher, perhaps thirty litres a minute against about twenty-one. That's a big reason maximal oxygen uptake rises: the most oxygen the body can take in and use each minute. It depends on two things: how much oxygenated blood the heart delivers, and how much the muscles extract, helped by more capillaries and mitochondria. What about the lungs? Lung size and how much air you can breathe out after a full breath barely change. But in healthy people at sea level, the lungs aren't the limit. Delivery and extraction are.

scenes.title: haemoglobin: more in total, thinner in concentration

voiceover.text: Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells, and it hides a trap. Endurance training raises total blood volume, and the liquid part, plasma, rises first and by more than the red cells do. So a trained athlete carries more haemoglobin in total, but their concentration can look normal or even a little low. Say an untrained person has a hundred and fifty grams per litre in five litres of blood. That's seven hundred and fifty grams. A trained athlete has a hundred and forty-five grams per litre, but in five point six litres. That's eight hundred and twelve grams. Lower concentration, more in total. It's dilution, not a deficiency. Thinner blood flows more easily, and there's more fluid for sweating to keep cool.

In muscle, hypertrophy means fibres getting bigger, not more numerous, and it raises the force a muscle can produce. It comes from overloading resistance training. But a beginner's first four to eight weeks of strength gains come mostly from the nervous system, recruiting fibres better, before size changes much. You met the two fibre types in Year 11, slow twitch and fast twitch, and that their mix is mostly inherited. What training changes is inside each type, not which type it is. Aerobic training gives slow fibres more mitochondria, capillaries and aerobic enzymes. Heavy and explosive training makes fast fibres grow and fire better. That's specificity again: fibres adapt to how they're used.

scenes.title: the chain, both ways, and reading the evidence

voiceover.text: The dot point asks you to examine a relationship. That's a chain with three links: a principle is applied, it produces an adaptation, and the adaptation improves performance. Aerobic volume, overloaded between the two thresholds, enlarges the left ventricle and raises stroke volume, so race pace sits at a lower share of maximum aerobic capacity and can be held longer. But here's the subtle part. An adaptation only improves performance if it improves what limits that athlete. And the chain runs backwards too. Stop training, and reversibility takes the adaptation away first. Coaches read these as evidence too, but illness, poor sleep and fatigue also raise resting heart rate. One number moving the wrong way is a question, not an answer.
Two things to remember. Each beat gets bigger, so fewer are needed. And principle, adaptation, performance: three links, every time.

Two exam questions. First. Complete each chain. One: twelve weeks of progressive overload in resistance training, above the strength threshold. Give the adaptation and the performance outcome. Two: an athlete's usual training run now feels easy, and their heart rate stays under sixty-five per cent of maximum heart rate. Give the adaptation, and the principle this now raises. Pause here to answer.

Chain A: first neural adaptation, then hypertrophy of fast twitch fibres, giving more force, like a harder tackle or a faster first step. Chain B: stroke volume has risen, so the same run needs fewer beats. The run is now below their threshold, so apply progressive overload. The classic mistake is naming the adaptation without the other links.

Second. A runner's sixteen-week record is on screen: resting heart rate, heart rate at a fixed pace, recovery, haemoglobin and sleep. Which measures show adaptation by week eight, why isn't the haemoglobin fall a problem, and what does week sixteen suggest? Pause here to answer.

By week eight, resting heart rate and heart rate at a fixed pace both fell, and recovery got faster: a bigger stroke volume. Haemoglobin concentration fell because plasma rose more, so it's dilution. By week sixteen, resting heart rate rose and recovery slowed. That points to fatigue outrunning recovery, the overload failure mode. The classic mistake is reading the haemoglobin as anaemia.

So name the principle, the adaptation and the performance it changes, and check it's that athlete's limiter. Every adaptation here starts the same way. A principle has to be applied, in a real session, on a real day. How do you start designing a training session?
